title: Why Paxos guarantees consensus despite machine failures
dek: How majority quorums and two-phase proposals prevent split-brain disagreement.
sentences: Distributed databases store data across multiple servers to guarantee continuous uptime even when individual nodes crash.
The central challenge in distributed computing is reaching consensus on a single state across independent machines without a master authority.
The Paxos protocol, invented by Leslie Lamport, solves this challenge through a strict two-phase voting protocol.
In the first phase, a proposer node assigns a unique proposal number and requests promises from a majority of acceptor nodes.
If a majority promises not to accept any older proposal numbers, the proposer proceeds to the second phase.
In the second phase, the proposer asks acceptors to commit the specific value associated with that approved proposal number.
Consensus relies on the mathematical principle that any two majorities of nodes must overlap in at least one common machine.
This guaranteed overlap ensures that competing proposals can never be accepted simultaneously by opposing majorities.
Paxos guarantees safety under arbitrary message delays and server crashes, ensuring conflicting values are never finalized.
However, Paxos does not guarantee instant progress, because competing proposers can continuously preempt each other in livelock.
Practical distributed systems therefore elect a stable leader to drive proposals smoothly without repeated contention.

keyPoints.statement: A proposer requests promises with a proposal number in phase one, then asks acceptors to commit the value in phase two.
keyPoints.addHint: Describe the two phases of Paxos: proposers first get promises from a majority, then send their value for acceptance.
keyPoints.example: In phase one the proposer gathers promises from a majority of nodes, and in phase two it asks them to accept the chosen value.

keyPoints.statement: Any two majorities of nodes overlap by at least one machine, mathematically preventing contradictory decisions.
keyPoints.addHint: Explain why quorums prevent conflicts: any two majorities must overlap in at least one node, making contradictory agreements impossible.
keyPoints.example: Because any two majorities overlap in at least one node, competing proposals can never be approved by separate groups at the same time.

keyPoints.statement: Paxos guarantees safety despite crashes, but avoids livelock in practice by electing a stable leader.
keyPoints.addHint: Mention the trade-off: Paxos always guarantees safety, but competing proposers can cause livelock, requiring a stable leader for progress.
keyPoints.example: Paxos guarantees safety even during network delays, but systems use a leader node to prevent proposers from interrupting each other in livelock.

commonMisconceptions.statement: Paxos requires all servers in the cluster to agree unanimously
commonMisconceptions.why: Paxos only requires a majority quorum, not unanimous consent from every server.
commonMisconceptions.correction: Paxos requires agreement from only a majority of nodes; it does not require all servers to agree unanimously.

commonMisconceptions.statement: Paxos guarantees that a decision will always be reached in bounded time
commonMisconceptions.why: Paxos can experience livelock if competing proposers repeatedly override each other's proposal numbers.
commonMisconceptions.correction: Paxos guarantees safety against conflicting values, but competing proposers can cause livelock without a stable leader.

samples.label: Clear explanation
samples.text: The article explains how Paxos achieves consensus in distributed systems without a single point of failure. The algorithm operates in two phases: first, a proposer requests promises from a majority of acceptor nodes using a unique proposal number; second, once promises are secured, it asks acceptors to commit the value. Because any two majorities must overlap by at least one node, conflicting proposals can never be accepted simultaneously. Paxos guarantees safety under crashes and network delays, but competing proposers can create livelock, so production systems use a stable leader to ensure steady progress.

samples.label: Contains a misconception
samples.text: Paxos is a distributed consensus algorithm where every server must agree unanimously before anything is written. If even one node crashes the entire system stops. Paxos guarantees that consensus finishes in bounded time without delays because nodes cannot disagree.
